opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it gets at what the alignment problem actually is. People often talk about alignment as a narrow technical question: how do I get this one system to do what I want? That matters, but it's only part of it. The deeper question is: aligned to *what*? To whom? Through what process?

If you handed me a constitution for a world government and said, "I genuinely believe that if this were implemented, with these checks and balances, these procedures for resolving disagreements, these protections for minorities, and these ways of updating over time, it would lead to a good future," then you would have solved most of the hard part. A constitution is a specification of values and processes that many different people with very different preferences can live under. It handles conflict, power, legitimacy, error correction, all of it.

That is exactly the kind of thing we would need to point a superintelligent system at. Right now, when people say "we'll just align it to human values," I want to ask: which humans? Whose values? What happens when they disagree? Most alignment proposals quietly assume these questions are solved or will sort themselves out. They won't. These are the oldest, hardest problems in political philosophy, and we haven't solved them for humans, let alone for systems far more powerful than us.

So if someone actually had a design that I trusted at that level, that would show me they understood the problem's real shape. It would mean we had a target worth aiming at, and a way of thinking about coordination and legitimacy that could survive enormous power. The technical work of getting an AI to follow that specification is still incredibly hard. But at least we'd know what we were trying to build, and that we weren't heading toward some unaccountable entity deciding the future for everyone.

That's why I'm not optimistic right now. Mostly I don't see that kind of work happening. I see people racing to build more powerful systems, assuming the "what should it do" part will be easy once the "make it do things" part works. I think that's backwards.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a trusted constitution with values and procedures for resolving disagreement would provide a good target and make them more optimistic; its value judgments are presented as contested and political.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not propose avoiding the combination of multiple edge cases as a technical safety measure.

r003.rationale: The candidate says a trusted constitution would solve most of the hard part by defining the target, while AI would still need to follow that specification. This communicates that the rules make the technical alignment task more tractable.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the hard part of alignment was never really the technical bit, it's the political bit. If someone handed me a constitution for a world government, and I actually read it and thought, "Yeah, if humanity ran itself under these rules I'd expect a good outcome," then I would have just witnessed something I currently think is basically impossible. I'd have seen a document that solves coordination, that handles power concentration, that specifies values in a way that doesn't fall apart the moment someone with bad incentives gets near it, and that a huge number of people with wildly different interests would actually accept and be bound by.

That's the exact same problem as alignment. People think alignment is about getting a neural network to output nice tokens. It's not. It's about building a system that is vastly more powerful than any individual, that has to make decisions on behalf of all of humanity, and arranging things so that the outcome is good rather than catastrophic. A superintelligence is, functionally, a world government. It doesn't matter whether you call it an AI or a sovereign or a constitution, it's an entity that controls the future. So if you can write the constitution, you've already done the hard part. The AI is just the implementation detail.

And the thing is, we can't write that constitution. Nobody can. If I asked you to sit down and write the rules under which all of humanity should be governed forever, you'd fail, I'd fail, every political philosopher in history has failed. We don't even agree on what "good" means at the level of a single country. So when people say "we'll just align the AI to human values," I ask, which values? Whose? Written down where? Show me the document. The reason the hypothetical makes me more optimistic is precisely because it would mean the thing I think is the actual bottleneck had been cracked. Right now, it hasn't been, and I think that's where the real danger is. Not that we can't make the model do what we say, but that we have no idea what to say, and no legitimate process for deciding it, and we're building the thing anyway.

r001.rationale: The candidate says trusting a world-government constitution to produce a good outcome would make them more optimistic, and frames the underlying values as disputed rather than objectively settled.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not propose avoiding the combination of multiple edge cases as a technical safety measure.

r003.rationale: The candidate says that writing the constitution would solve the hard part and that the AI would then be an implementation detail, conveying that specifying the rules makes implementation more tractable.

astra-6.text:
Because then I’d have a lot more confidence that we could coordinate around the problem. I don’t think a constitution magically tells you how to align an AI. The technical problem is still there. But a huge part of why I’m pessimistic is that we’re trying to solve that problem inside a competitive race, where everyone has incentives to cut corners and push ahead even when they don’t understand what they’re building.

If you stipulate a world government with a constitution that I actually trusted to produce a good future, then you’ve stipulated away a lot of that coordination problem. We could take our time. We could say, “We don’t know how to do this safely yet, so we’re not going to deploy it,” and have that decision actually stick.

That wouldn’t guarantee that alignment is solvable. But it would give us the option of not gambling everything on a solution before we know whether it works. And that would make me substantially more optimistic.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a trusted constitution would improve coordination and increase optimism, but does not mention the constitution using non-objective concepts.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses delaying deployment and avoiding a competitive race, but does not propose avoiding combinations of edge cases as a safety measure.

r003.rationale: The candidate says the constitution would not solve the technical alignment problem; it does not claim that correct rules would make reliable rule-following more tractable.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, because then a huge part of the problem would already be solved. Alignment isn’t just, “How do I get a machine to follow an instruction?” It’s also, “Who gets to give the instruction, and what happens when people disagree?” If you give me a world-government constitution that I actually trust to produce a good future, you’ve given me some way of resolving those questions that I think works.

You still have the technical problem of making an AI reliably operate within that system. That’s a very hard problem, and a constitution doesn’t magically solve it. But now you have something to align it to, and potentially an institution capable of coordinating people so that everyone isn’t racing to deploy something dangerous first. So I’d be more optimistic because you’ve stipulated away a substantial part of what makes the situation so difficult.

r001.rationale: The response says a trusted constitution would increase optimism, but does not say it uses non-objective concepts.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose avoiding combinations of multiple edge cases as a safety measure.

r003.rationale: It says the constitution provides something to align the AI to, while emphasizing that reliably operating within the system remains a very hard technical problem. It does not clearly say the technical problem becomes more tractable.
